questions.title: Q1 — Homogeneous coordinates
questions.prompt:
(a) Write the Cartesian point (3, 4) in two different homogeneous forms, and convert (6, 9, 3)^T back to Cartesian coordinates. [2 marks]
(b) Find the line l through (1, 1) and (3, 5) using a cross product. [2 marks]
(c) Find the intersection of l with the line x = 0, whose homogeneous line vector is (1, 0, 0)^T. [2 marks]
Show your working.
questions.solution:
(a) (3, 4, 1)^T and (6, 8, 2)^T represent (3, 4); (6, 9, 3)^T becomes (2, 3).
(b) (1, 1, 1) × (3, 5, 1) = (-4, 2, 2), giving -4x + 2y + 2 = 0, or y = 2x - 1.
(c) (-4, 2, 2) × (1, 0, 0) = (0, 2, -2). Divide by -2 to obtain (0, -1).
Equivalent non-zero homogeneous scalings are acceptable.

questions.title: Q2 — Transformation hierarchy
questions.prompt:
(a) State the degrees of freedom of a 2D Euclidean, similarity, affine and projective transformation. [4 marks]
(b) For each, state which of these are preserved: parallelism, ratios of lengths on a line, angles, and cross-ratio. [2 marks]
(c) How many point correspondences are needed to estimate a 2D homography, and why? State the non-degeneracy requirement. [2 marks]
questions.solution:
(a) Euclidean: 3; similarity: 4; affine: 6; projective: 8.
(b) Euclidean and similarity preserve all four listed properties. Affine preserves parallelism, ratios on a line and cross-ratio, but not angles. A general projective transformation preserves cross-ratio but not the other three.
(c) Four point pairs in general position (no three collinear in either plane). A 3 × 3 homography has 9 entries minus one arbitrary scale = 8 degrees of freedom; each pair gives two independent equations.

questions.title: Q3 — Rotation matrices
questions.prompt:
Let R be the rotation of +90 degrees about the z-axis, acting on column vectors.
(a) Write R and verify R^T R = I and det(R) = 1. [3 marks]
(b) Compute R^(-1) without a general matrix inversion, and apply R to (1, 2, 3)^T. [2 marks]
(c) A rotation Rx(+90 degrees) is applied after R. Write the combined matrix and explain whether the order matters. [3 marks]
questions.solution:
(a) R = [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]]. Its columns are orthonormal, so R^T R = I, and det(R) = 1.
(b) R^(-1) = R^T = [[0, 1, 0], [-1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1]]. Applying R gives (-2, 1, 3)^T.
(c) Rx = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]]. The combined matrix is Rx R = [[0, -1, 0], [0, 0, -1], [1, 0, 0]]. Reversing the order gives a different result.

questions.title: Q4 — Shared camera data
questions.prompt:
A pinhole camera has focal length f = 8 mm, square pixels of size 5 micrometres, and a 1280 × 960 pixel sensor. Take the principal point at (width/2, height/2), with no skew.
The point in camera coordinates is (X, Y, Z) = (0.5, -0.2, 5) metres.

questions.title: Q4(a) — Focal length in pixels
questions.prompt: Calculate the common focal length fx = fy in pixels. Enter a number only.
questions.solution: 5 micrometres = 0.005 mm. fx = fy = 8 / 0.005 = 1600 pixels.

questions.title: Q4(a) — Intrinsic matrix K
questions.prompt: Write the camera intrinsic matrix K. Show how you obtain the principal point and focal lengths.

questions.title: Q4(b) — Projected u-coordinate
questions.prompt: Project the given camera-frame point. Enter its image u-coordinate in pixels.

questions.title: Q4(b) — Projected v-coordinate
questions.prompt: Project the given camera-frame point. Enter its image v-coordinate in pixels.

questions.title: Q4(c) — Effect of doubling depth
questions.prompt: The point moves to Z = 10 m while X and Y remain fixed. What happens to its image offset from the principal point? Explain.
questions.solution: The offsets halve because they are proportional to 1/Z. At Z = 5 m they are (160, -64) px; at Z = 10 m they are (80, -32) px, giving image position (720, 448).

questions.title: Q5 — Shared camera pose
questions.prompt:
K = [[800, 0, 320], [0, 800, 240], [0, 0, 1]], R = I, and the camera centre is C = (0, 0, -2)^T.
Use Xc = R Xw + t and P = K[R | t]. The world point to project is Xw = (0.25, 0.125, 3)^T.

questions.title: Q5(a) — Translation and projection matrix
questions.prompt: Find t and write P = K[R | t]. Show your working.

questions.title: Q5(b) — World point projection u
questions.prompt: Project the given world point. Enter the image u-coordinate in pixels.

questions.title: Q5(b) — World point projection v
questions.prompt: Project the given world point. Enter the image v-coordinate in pixels.

questions.title: Q5(c) — Projection matrix degrees of freedom
questions.prompt: Explain why a general 3 × 4 camera projection matrix P has 11 degrees of freedom.
questions.solution: There are 12 matrix entries, but multiplying the whole matrix by a non-zero scale does not change the projective mapping. Therefore 12 - 1 = 11 independent parameters.

questions.title: Q6 — Shared road measurement data
questions.prompt:
A forward-looking camera views a planar road. Ground coordinates are in centimetres.
The ground-to-image homography is H = [[2, 0, 100], [0, 1, 50], [0, 0.002, 1]].
The left and right kerb pixels are (200, 200) and (600, 200). Use the inverse homography followed by division by the homogeneous scale to recover ground coordinates.

questions.title: Q6(a) — Invert the road homography
questions.prompt: Compute H^(-1). A non-zero scalar multiple is acceptable. Show your working.
questions.solution:
det(H) = 2(1 - 50 × 0.002) = 1.8.
adj(H) = [[0.9, 0.2, -100], [0, 2, -100], [0, -0.004, 2]].
H^(-1) = adj(H)/1.8. The adjugate alone gives the same Cartesian mapping after the perspective divide.

questions.title: Q6(b) — Left kerb ground X
questions.prompt: Map the left kerb pixel to the road. Enter its ground X-coordinate in centimetres.

questions.title: Q6(b) — Left kerb ground Y
questions.prompt: Map the left kerb pixel to the road. Enter its ground Y-coordinate in centimetres.

questions.title: Q6(b) — Right kerb ground X
questions.prompt: Map the right kerb pixel to the road. Enter its ground X-coordinate in centimetres.

questions.title: Q6(b) — Right kerb ground Y
questions.prompt: Map the right kerb pixel to the road. Enter its ground Y-coordinate in centimetres.

questions.title: Q6(c) — Road width in metres
questions.prompt: Calculate the road width. Enter your answer in metres, not centimetres or pixels.
questions.solution: The ground points are (100, 250) cm and (400, 250) cm. Their distance is 300 cm = 3 m.

questions.title: Q6(c) — Why pixel subtraction is insufficient
questions.prompt: Why would simply subtracting the horizontal pixel coordinates, giving 400 pixels, not give the physical road width?
questions.solution: Perspective scale depends on position/depth. A pixel distance is not a metric distance. The calibrated inverse homography maps both endpoints into ground coordinates in known units; a single global pixels-to-centimetres factor is generally invalid.

questions.title: Q7 — Shared surgical measurement data
questions.prompt:
A calibrated overhead camera views a planar operating field. Field coordinates are in millimetres.
The field-to-image homography is H = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0.002, 0.001, 1]].
An instrument's tip and tail appear at pixels (250, 0) and (125, 250). Assume both lie in the calibrated plane.

questions.title: Q7(a) — Invert the surgical homography
questions.prompt: Write H^(-1) and verify your result.
questions.solution: H^(-1) = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [-0.002, -0.001, 1]]. Multiplying by H cancels the two off-diagonal entries in the third row, yielding I.

questions.title: Q7(b) — Tip X-coordinate
questions.prompt: Inverse-map the instrument tip. Enter X in millimetres.

questions.title: Q7(b) — Tip Y-coordinate
questions.prompt: Inverse-map the instrument tip. Enter Y in millimetres.
questions.solution: The tip's homogeneous result is (250, 0, 0.5)^T. Y = 0/0.5 = 0 mm.

questions.title: Q7(b) — Tail X-coordinate
questions.prompt: Inverse-map the instrument tail. Enter X in millimetres.

questions.title: Q7(b) — Tail Y-coordinate
questions.prompt: Inverse-map the instrument tail. Enter Y in millimetres.
questions.solution: The tail's homogeneous result is (125, 250, 0.5)^T. Y = 250/0.5 = 500 mm.

questions.title: Q7(c) — Instrument length
questions.prompt: Calculate the instrument length in millimetres. Round to one decimal place.

questions.title: Q7(c) — Measurement errors and calibration
questions.prompt: Give two reasons the measured length may be wrong by several millimetres in practice and one way to improve the four-point calibration.
questions.solution: Possible errors: inaccurate endpoint/calibration-point localisation; unmodelled lens distortion; instrument endpoints not lying in the calibrated plane. Improve calibration using more than four well-distributed reference points and an overdetermined least-squares fit (with outlier handling when appropriate).

questions.title: Q8 — Shared pure-rotation camera data
questions.prompt:
K = [[800, 0, 320], [0, 800, 240], [0, 0, 1]]. The camera rotates about its centre with no translation. Use Ry(10 degrees) = [[cos(10°), 0, sin(10°)], [0, 1, 0], [-sin(10°), 0, cos(10°)]] for the mapping from image 1 rays to image 2 rays.
The image 1 principal point is (320, 240). Both views have the same K.

questions.title: Q8(a) — Pure rotation homography
questions.prompt: Give the formula for the homography H mapping image 1 to image 2.
questions.solution: H = K R K^(-1), where R is the stated rotation of image 1 rays into image 2 coordinates.

questions.title: Q8(b) — Rotated principal point u
questions.prompt: Where does the image 1 principal point appear in image 2? Enter the u-coordinate in pixels, to one decimal place.

questions.title: Q8(b) — Rotated principal point v
questions.prompt: Where does the image 1 principal point appear in image 2? Enter the v-coordinate in pixels.
questions.solution: The rotated normalised ray has zero y component, so v = 800 × 0 + 240 = 240 px.

questions.title: Q8(c) — Why pure rotation gives no depth
questions.prompt: Why can depth not be recovered by triangulation from two images related by pure rotation about the camera centre?
questions.solution: The views share the same camera centre, so there is no translational baseline or parallax. H = K R K^(-1) has no depth term; points at different distances along the same ray transform identically.

questions.title: Q9 — Direct Linear Transform
questions.prompt:
(a) How many independent equations does each 3D–2D correspondence give for P, and what is the minimum number of points? [3 marks]
(b) Explain how SVD solves A p = 0, and why normalising points helps. [3 marks]
(c) Name one degenerate configuration of the 3D points and explain the effect. [2 marks]
(d) How are K, R and t recovered from P = [M | p4]? [2 marks]
questions.solution:
(a) Two equations per point; at least six non-degenerate 3D–2D correspondences for the 11 degrees of freedom of P.
(b) Form a 2n × 12 matrix A. In A = U Σ V^T, choose the last column of V (smallest singular value) and reshape it to 3 × 4. Normalise centroids to zero and mean distances to sqrt(2) in 2D / sqrt(3) in 3D to improve conditioning; denormalise the resulting P.
(c) All 3D points on a plane is degenerate for a general camera matrix: P is not uniquely determined.
(d) RQ-decompose M = K R, enforce the chosen sign/scale conventions, then t = K^(-1) p4.

questions.title: Q10 — Essential matrix and epipolar lines
questions.prompt:
Two normalised cameras have R = I and translation direction t = (0, 0, 1)^T, representing motion along the optical axis. Use E = [t]× R.
(a) Write E. [3 marks]
(b) For x = (0.2, 0.1, 1)^T in image 1, compute the epipolar line l' = E x in image 2. [3 marks]
(c) Where are the epipoles? What is distinctive about epipolar lines for this forward-motion geometry? [4 marks]
questions.solution:
(a) E = [[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]], up to non-zero scale.
(b) l' = (-0.1, 0.2, 0)^T, giving -0.1x' + 0.2y' = 0, or y' = 0.5x'.
(c) Both epipoles are (0, 0, 1)^T, the principal point in normalised coordinates. Epipolar lines radiate through it rather than being parallel horizontal lines. Changing the sign of E does not change the lines.

questions.title: Q11 — Fundamental matrix
questions.prompt:
(a) State the epipolar constraint and the relation between the fundamental matrix F and essential matrix E. [3 marks]
(b) Give the degrees of freedom of E and F and explain why det(F) = 0. Assume a non-zero stereo baseline. [3 marks]
(c) How many correspondences does the linear 8-point algorithm need, and which step enforces rank 2? [2 marks]
questions.solution:
(a) x'^T F x = 0 for corresponding pixel points. F = K'^(-T) E K^(-1), equivalently E = K'^T F K.
(b) E has 5 degrees of freedom: 3 for rotation and 2 for translation direction up to scale. F has 7: 9 entries minus scale and the determinant constraint. Its epipolar construction includes a rank-2 skew-symmetric factor, so det(F) = 0.
(c) At least 8 correspondences. After SVD of the estimate, set its smallest singular value to zero and reconstruct F.

questions.title: Q12 — Rectification and triangulation
questions.prompt:
(a) What does standard horizontal stereo rectification do to the epipolar lines and epipoles? [3 marks]
(b) Why does this reduce stereo matching to a 1D search? [2 marks]
(c) Four (R, t) decompositions of E exist. How is the physically correct one selected using chirality? [3 marks]
questions.solution:
(a) Corresponding epipolar lines become horizontal and aligned by image row; epipoles lie at infinity along the horizontal direction, (1, 0, 0)^T.
(b) Correspondences are on the same row, leaving only a horizontal displacement to search.
(c) The four candidates are (R1, ±t) and (R2, ±t). Triangulate correspondences and choose the candidate putting points in front of both cameras, with positive camera-frame depth.

questions.title: Q13 — Shared stereo rig (stimulus example)
questions.prompt:
Use this same setup for all linked Q13 questions:
A rectified stereo rig has focal length f = 1000 pixels and baseline B = 0.2 metres.
Disparity is measured in pixels and depth in metres.

questions.title: Q13(a) — Depth at disparity 40 px
questions.prompt: Calculate the depth for disparity d = 40 px. Enter metres as a number only.

questions.title: Q13(a) — Depth at disparity 25 px
questions.prompt: Calculate the depth for disparity d = 25 px. Enter metres as a number only.

questions.title: Q13(a) — Depth at disparity 10 px
questions.prompt: Calculate the depth for disparity d = 10 px. Enter metres as a number only.

questions.title: Q13(b) — Depth precision at 20 m
questions.prompt: At Z = 20 m, estimate the magnitude of the depth uncertainty for a disparity error of ±1 px. Use first-order error propagation and enter the positive uncertainty in metres.
questions.solution: |ΔZ| ≈ Z^2 |Δd| / (fB) = 20^2 × 1 / (1000 × 0.2) = 2 m. The exact errors at disparities 9 and 11 px are asymmetric; this question asks for the first-order approximation.

questions.title: Q13(c) — Doubling the baseline
questions.prompt: If the baseline is doubled, explain the effects on range, depth precision and matching difficulty.
questions.solution: At a fixed disparity the measurable depth doubles. At fixed depth and disparity-error magnitude, uncertainty halves (2 m becomes 1 m at Z = 20 m). Larger baseline increases disparities and required search range, can increase occlusions, and reduces overlap at close range.

questions.title: Q14 — Shared block-matching windows
questions.prompt:
The 3 × 3 left window is L = [[10, 20, 30], [40, 50, 60], [70, 80, 90]].
The candidate right windows are:
R0 = [[12, 22, 28], [38, 52, 61], [72, 79, 93]];
R1 = [[50, 60, 70], [80, 90, 100], [10, 20, 30]].
SAD sums absolute pixel differences. SSD sums squared pixel differences.

questions.title: Q14(a) — SAD for R0
questions.prompt: Calculate SAD(L, R0). Enter an integer.
questions.solution: Absolute differences: [[2,2,2],[2,2,1],[2,1,3]]. Their sum is 17.

questions.title: Q14(a) — SSD for R0
questions.prompt: Calculate SSD(L, R0). Enter an integer.
questions.solution: Squared differences: [[4,4,4],[4,4,1],[4,1,9]]. Their sum is 35.

questions.title: Q14(a) — SAD for R1
questions.prompt: Calculate SAD(L, R1). Enter an integer.
questions.solution: Six absolute differences are 40 and three are 60. SAD = 6 × 40 + 3 × 60 = 420.

questions.title: Q14(a) — SSD for R1
questions.prompt: Calculate SSD(L, R1). Enter an integer.

questions.title: Q14(b) — Winner-takes-all selection
questions.prompt: Which candidate's disparity is selected by winner-takes-all? Explain using the costs.
questions.solution: Choose the disparity corresponding to R0 because it minimises both SAD (17 < 420) and SSD (35 < 20400). The actual pixel displacement is not specified; the answer is the R0 candidate.

questions.title: Q14(c) — SSD and outliers
questions.prompt: Why are SSD costs more sensitive to outliers than SAD costs?
questions.solution: SSD squares residuals, so one large mismatch can dominate the sum. SAD grows only linearly with residual magnitude. Specular highlights or occlusion can create such large residuals.

questions.title: Q14(d) — Window-matching failure cases
questions.prompt: Name two image conditions in which this local window-matching approach can fail, and briefly explain why.
questions.solution: Textureless regions give a flat or ambiguous cost curve. Repeating patterns give several similar minima. Occlusions, depth discontinuities and brightness differences can also violate the matching assumptions. Any two appropriate explanations.

questions.title: Q15 — Local versus global stereo methods
questions.prompt:
(a) Explain the effect of window size on accuracy at depth edges and in low-texture regions. [3 marks]
(b) What do the smoothness penalties P1 and P2 add in scanline/semi-global methods? [3 marks]
(c) Describe a left–right consistency check and which pixels it rejects. [2 marks]
(d) A flat wall with a repeating tile pattern is labelled at the wrong depth. Diagnose the problem and suggest two remedies. [2 marks]
questions.solution:
(a) Small windows preserve sharper boundaries but are noisy/ambiguous in weak texture. Larger windows add support but mix depths and blur/fatten boundaries.
(b) P1 penalises a disparity change of one; P2 penalises larger changes, usually more strongly. Smoothness encourages coherent surfaces while balancing evidence for real depth changes.
(c) Match in both directions. With a consistent positive-disparity convention, reject where |dL(x) - dR(x - dL(x))| exceeds a tolerance (often 1 px). These are commonly occlusions or mismatches.
(d) Repeated texture creates ambiguous periodic matches. Remedies include a suitable larger support region, SGM/global constraints, a physically justified search range, added texture/structured light, or a consistency check. A consistency check does not guarantee removal of mutually consistent wrong matches.

questions.title: Q16 — Shared checkerboard calibration data
questions.prompt:
A planar checkerboard lies on Zw = 0, with board coordinates in millimetres.
K = [[1000, 0, 500], [0, 1000, 400], [0, 0, 1]].
R = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0.8, -0.6], [0, 0.6, 0.8]].
t = (0, 50, 1000)^T mm.
The board-to-image homography is H = K[r1 | r2 | t], where r1 and r2 are the first two columns of R. The board corner to project is (100, 100) mm.

questions.title: Q16(a) — Checkerboard homography
questions.prompt: Calculate the 3 × 3 homography H = K[r1 | r2 | t], relating (X, Y, 1)^T on the board to image pixels (u, v, 1)^T up to scale. Show the matrix multiplication.

questions.title: Q16(b) — Checkerboard corner u
questions.prompt: Project the checkerboard corner. Enter u in pixels, to one decimal place.

questions.title: Q16(b) — Checkerboard corner v
questions.prompt: Project the checkerboard corner. Enter v in pixels, to one decimal place.
questions.solution: The homogeneous image point is (630,554,1.06)^T. v = 554/1.06 = 522.6415... px, or 522.6 px.

questions.title: Q16(c) — Zhang's two constraints
questions.prompt:
For the first two columns h1 and h2 of H, explain the geometric origin of:
h1^T K^(-T) K^(-1) h2 = 0,
and
h1^T K^(-T) K^(-1) h1 = h2^T K^(-T) K^(-1) h2.
questions.solution: Up to a common scale λ, h1 = λ K r1 and h2 = λ K r2. The first constraint follows from r1 and r2 being orthogonal. The second follows from their equal unit lengths. These are properties of the first two columns of a rotation matrix.

questions.title: Q17 — Shared fundamental matrix and feature
questions.prompt:
A stereo rig has fundamental matrix F = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, -0.04], [0, 0.04, 0]].
The Image 1 point is x = (250, 200, 1)^T.
Candidate Image 2 points are x'A = (180, 200, 1)^T and x'B = (180, 210, 1)^T.

questions.title: Q17(a) — Determinant of F
questions.prompt: Evaluate det(F).
questions.solution: The first row is zero, so det(F) = 0.

questions.title: Q17(a) — Rank of F
questions.prompt: State the rank of F. Enter an integer.
questions.solution: Rows 2 and 3 are non-zero and independent, while row 1 is zero. Therefore rank(F) = 2.

questions.title: Q17(a) — Verify determinant and rank
questions.prompt: Show why the determinant is zero and justify the rank using the matrix's rows or columns.
questions.solution: The zero first row forces determinant zero. Rows (0,0,-0.04) and (0,0.04,0) are linearly independent; therefore the rank is exactly 2, not merely at most 2.

questions.title: Q17(b) — Epipole at infinity
questions.prompt: Find e' satisfying F^T e' = 0. Show that it lies at infinity and explain the implication for the epipolar geometry.
questions.solution: For e' = (a,b,c)^T, F^T e' = 0 gives 0.04c = 0 and -0.04b = 0. Thus e' = (1,0,0)^T up to scale. Its last coordinate is zero: it is at horizontal infinity, so epipolar lines are parallel and horizontal (rectified-type geometry). F alone does not uniquely establish the physical camera pose or calibration.

questions.title: Q17(c) — Algebraic epipolar line
questions.prompt: Determine l' = F x = (a,b,c)^T and write the algebraic equation of the corresponding epipolar line in Image 2.
questions.solution: F(250,200,1)^T = (0,-0.04,8)^T. Therefore -0.04v' + 8 = 0, or v' = 200. An equivalent line vector is (0,1,-200)^T.

questions.title: Q17(d) — Test point incidence
questions.prompt: Test whether candidate A or B lies on the epipolar line corresponding to x. Show the incidence calculation for each candidate.
questions.solution: The line is v' = 200. Using (0,1,-200), A gives 200-200 = 0 and lies on the line. B gives 210-200 = 10 and does not. Using unnormalised F x gives 0 and -0.4 respectively; both scalings are valid.

questions.title: Q18 — Shared calibrated stereo geometry
questions.prompt:
Both cameras have K = I and relative orientation R = I. Camera 2's centre in Camera 1 coordinates is t = (0.2, 0, 0)^T metres, so a point transforms as P2 = R^T(P1 - t).
The observed normalised image points are x1 = (0.10, 0.05, 1)^T and x2 = (0.06, 0.05, 1)^T.
For this R = I case, use the essential-matrix representative E = [t]×R. E and -E encode the same epipolar constraint.

questions.title: Q18(a) — Skew matrix and essential matrix
questions.prompt: Construct the skew-symmetric matrix [t]× and compute E = [t]×R.
questions.solution: [t]× = [[0,0,0],[0,0,-0.2],[0,0.2,0]]. Since R = I, this is also the requested representative of E. With the standard world-to-camera translation -t, the essential matrix has the opposite sign, which is projectively equivalent.

questions.title: Q18(b) — Epipolar constraint value
questions.prompt: Evaluate the scalar x2^T E x1.

questions.title: Q18(b) — Verify the epipolar constraint
questions.prompt: Show the multiplication E x1 and then x2^T E x1 to verify the epipolar constraint.
questions.solution: E x1 = (0,-0.2,0.01)^T. Then x2^T E x1 = 0 - 0.01 + 0.01 = 0. The image points satisfy the epipolar constraint.

questions.title: Q18(c) — Triangulated X
questions.prompt: Triangulate the point. Enter its X-coordinate in metres relative to Camera 1.

questions.title: Q18(c) — Triangulated Y
questions.prompt: Triangulate the point. Enter its Y-coordinate in metres relative to Camera 1.

questions.title: Q18(c) — Triangulated Z
questions.prompt: Triangulate the point. Enter its Z-coordinate in metres relative to Camera 1.
questions.solution: For normalised coordinates f = 1. Z = B/(x1-x2) = 0.2/(0.10-0.06) = 5 m.

questions.title: Q18(c) — Verify chirality
questions.prompt: Verify that the triangulated point has positive depth in both cameras. Show the point in both camera coordinate systems.
questions.solution: P1 = (0.5,0.25,5) m. P2 = P1-t = (0.3,0.25,5) m. Z1 = Z2 = 5 > 0, so the point lies in front of both cameras.

questions.title: Q19 — Shared vehicle stereo specifications
questions.prompt:
An autonomous vehicle's stereo camera has f = 1500 pixels, baseline B = 0.40 m, and sensor resolution 1920 × 1080 pixels.
For depth uncertainty, use the first-order relation |ΔZ| ≈ Z^2 |Δd|/(fB). The disparity-error magnitude is 0.5 px where specified.

questions.title: Q19(a) — Pedestrian distance
questions.prompt: A pedestrian produces disparity d = 30.0 px. Calculate the distance Z in metres.

questions.title: Q19(b) — Uncertainty at 10 m
questions.prompt: For disparity error Δd = ±0.5 px, calculate the depth-uncertainty magnitude at Z = 10.0 m. Enter metres, to three decimal places.

questions.title: Q19(b) — Uncertainty at 40 m
questions.prompt: For disparity error Δd = ±0.5 px, calculate the depth-uncertainty magnitude at Z = 40.0 m. Enter metres, to two decimal places.

questions.title: Q19(c) — Minimum baseline
questions.prompt: The braking system requires |ΔZ| ≤ 1.5 m at Z = 30.0 m. With f = 1500 px and |Δd| = 0.5 px unchanged, determine the minimum required baseline in metres.
questions.solution: Z^2 |Δd|/(fB) ≤ 1.5 implies B ≥ Z^2 |Δd|/(1.5f) = 900×0.5/(1.5×1500) = 0.20 m. This is the minimum; the given 0.40 m baseline already exceeds it.

questions.title: Q20 — Shared DLT projection matrix
questions.prompt:
DLT yields P = [[800, 0, 320, -1600], [0, 800, 240, -1200], [0, 0, 1, -5]].
Use P = K[R | t] and denote its left 3 × 3 submatrix by M and its last column by p4.
Positions and translations are in the unspecified world-coordinate units used by P; focal lengths and principal-point coordinates are in pixels.

questions.title: Q20(a) — Optical centre X0
questions.prompt: Solve P(X0,Y0,Z0,1)^T = 0. Enter X0 in world-coordinate units.
questions.solution: Row 3 gives Z0 = 5. Row 1 gives 800X0 + 320×5 - 1600 = 0, so X0 = 0.

questions.title: Q20(a) — Optical centre Y0
questions.prompt: Solve P(X0,Y0,Z0,1)^T = 0. Enter Y0 in world-coordinate units.
questions.solution: Row 3 gives Z0 = 5. Row 2 gives 800Y0 + 240×5 - 1200 = 0, so Y0 = 0.

questions.title: Q20(a) — Optical centre Z0
questions.prompt: Solve P(X0,Y0,Z0,1)^T = 0. Enter Z0 in world-coordinate units.
questions.solution: The last row of P(X0,Y0,Z0,1)^T = 0 is Z0 - 5 = 0. Thus Z0 = 5 and Cw = (0,0,5).

questions.title: Q20(b) — Intrinsic and rotation decomposition
questions.prompt: Decompose M into K R, using positive focal lengths and K33 = 1. State K, R, the focal lengths, principal point and Euler rotation angles.
questions.solution:
M is already upper triangular with positive diagonal: K = [[800,0,320],[0,800,240],[0,0,1]] and R = I.
fx = fy = 800 px; (cx,cy) = (320,240) px. Euler rotation angles are all zero.

questions.title: Q20(c) — Translation tx
questions.prompt: Solve p4 = Kt. Enter tx in world-coordinate units.

questions.title: Q20(c) — Translation ty
questions.prompt: Solve p4 = Kt. Enter ty in world-coordinate units.

questions.title: Q20(c) — Translation tz
questions.prompt: Solve p4 = Kt. Enter tz in world-coordinate units.
questions.solution: The third row of Kt = p4 directly gives tz = -5. Thus t = (0,0,-5).

questions.title: Q20(c) — Verify the optical centre
questions.prompt: Using the recovered R and t, verify Cw = -R^T t and check that its homogeneous vector lies in the null space of P.
